core: working definition (MedlinePlus/NLM-attributed): oxygen saturation (O2 sat, SpO2) is the percentage of hemoglobin — the oxygen-carrying protein in red blood cells — that is carrying oxygen; the ATS describes it as the percentage of how much oxygen the blood is carrying compared to the maximum it is capable of carrying
normal adult reference range: roughly 95-100% on room air (MedlinePlus), attributed, with the honest note that chronic lung conditions (e.g., COPD) make lower saturations acceptable or even the goal

how it is measured: pulse oximetry — a small noninvasive clip on a fingertip that shines light through the skin and blood, reads the light that passes through, and returns a saturation percentage plus heart rate in seconds (MedlinePlus, OpenStax, Merck Manual, ATS)

why it matters: low oxygen saturation (hypoxemia) signals trouble — cells and organs cannot work properly the longer oxygen stays low, so a falling number is an early warning that prompts quick treatment, with an original example
what affects it, each named with one factual line: lung conditions, altitude, anemia
the limits, each named with one line: cold fingers, nail polish, motion — plus the honest note that readings can be off by a few percentage points
honest framing: SpO2 is a spotlight, not the whole picture — it measures saturation, not total oxygen; an arterial blood gas is more exact and adds carbon dioxide and acidity
supporting: a pulse oximeter also displays heart rate, and the reading appears after a few seconds (MedlinePlus)
readings can differ from the true blood oxygen level by about 2-4% (MedlinePlus) or about 2% over or under (ATS)
dark nail polish, artificial nails, darker skin pigmentation, poor circulation, cold skin, and movement can cause inaccurate results (MedlinePlus, ATS)
OpenStax corroborates the adult sea-level range as 94-98% and gives a COPD target of roughly 88-92%; MedlinePlus says lower levels may be acceptable with COPD or pneumonia
signs of low oxygen include bluish lips, nails, or face (cyanosis), trouble breathing, chest pain, and a fast heart rate (MedlinePlus)
MedlinePlus consumer guidance: contact a provider at 92% or lower; seek immediate medical attention at 88% or lower
an ABG directly measures oxygen saturation, the partial pressure of oxygen, carbon dioxide, and acidity from arterial blood (MedlinePlus, Merck Manual)
pulse oximetry is used before, during, and after surgery, for lung conditions, and for at-home monitoring in chronic lung disease (MedlinePlus)
outOfScope: respiratory rate, breathing patterns, and the mechanics of breathing (owned by nursing-and-allied-health-foundations:foundations:respirations)
the full vital-signs set, how to take each vital sign, and normal ranges for all of them (owned by nursing-and-allied-health-foundations:foundations:vital-signs)
respiratory physiology depth — gas exchange mechanics, the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve, and acid-base balance (owned by the biology subject)
oxygen therapy delivery systems and flow-rate decisions (not taught in this lesson)

claims.claim: Oxygen saturation (O2 sat, SpO2) is the percentage of hemoglobin — the oxygen-carrying protein in red blood cells — that is carrying oxygen; MedlinePlus describes the O2 sat measurement as how much oxygen the red blood cells are carrying, and the American Thoracic Society describes it as the percentage of how much oxygen the blood is carrying compared to the maximum it is capable of carrying.

A normal oxygen saturation level ranges between 95% and 100% on room air for healthy adults (MedlinePlus); OpenStax gives the adult sea-level normal as 94-98%, so the ranges overlap and vary slightly by source.

Chronic lung conditions change the picture: MedlinePlus states saturation levels may be somewhat lower and still considered acceptable with a lung disease such as COPD or pneumonia, and OpenStax gives an example target of roughly 88-92% for many COPD patients.

Pulse oximetry measures oxygen saturation noninvasively: a small clip-like device on a fingertip (or earlobe) shines light through the skin into the blood, a sensor reads the light that passes through, and the device calculates a saturation percentage and heart rate within seconds.

Low blood oxygen (hypoxemia) makes it hard for the body to work properly: MedlinePlus states the longer blood oxygen stays low, the higher the risk of damage to tissues and organs, so quick treatment of low blood oxygen helps avoid serious complications; the ATS adds that very low oxygen can strain the heart and brain.
Living at a higher elevation lowers oxygen saturation readings, and lower levels can still be normal there because the air holds less oxygen (MedlinePlus, OpenStax).
Anemia affects oxygen transport: with fewer red blood cells there are fewer carriers, so less oxygen is circulated; OpenStax notes that severe anemia can also make SpO2 readings inaccurate.

Several factors can make a pulse oximetry reading inaccurate: dark nail polish blocks the light, cold fingers and poor circulation weaken the signal, and movement can distort it; MedlinePlus says results may be 2% to 4% higher or lower than the actual blood oxygen level, and the ATS says most oximeters give a reading about 2% over or under.

Pulse oximetry measures oxygen saturation, not the total amount of oxygen in the blood, and it does not measure carbon dioxide; an arterial blood gas (ABG) directly measures blood oxygen, carbon dioxide, and acidity and is more exact than pulse oximetry (Merck Manual, MedlinePlus, ATS).

conflictingEvidence.issue: The normal saturation range varies slightly by source
positions: MedlinePlus: a normal oxygen saturation level ranges between 95% and 100%
OpenStax Clinical Nursing Skills: normal saturation at sea level is 94 to 98 percent
ATS patient sheet: 'normally, more than 89% of your red blood should be carrying oxygen' (a floor, not a range)
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches 95-100% on room air as the adult reference, attributed to MedlinePlus, and notes the range varies a little by source (OpenStax 94-98%) — so a point in the mid-90s is unremarkable under either.

conflictingEvidence.issue: What target is acceptable for chronic lung disease
positions: MedlinePlus: levels may be somewhat lower and considered acceptable with a lung disease such as COPD or pneumonia
OpenStax ch. 18: for COPD/emphysema a normal oxygen level is 88 to 90 percent; ch. 24: target may be lower at 88 to 92 percent
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson says lower targets are acceptable for chronic lung disease, cites OpenStax's roughly 88-92% as an example range, and notes the exact target is set by the care team — no single universal COPD number is taught.

positions: MedlinePlus: results may be 2% to 4% higher or lower than the actual blood oxygen level
ATS: most oximeters give a reading 2% over or under what an arterial blood gas would show
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states readings can differ from the true value by a few percentage points (roughly 2-4%), which covers both sources without false precision.

positions: MedlinePlus lists darker skin pigmentation among things that may cause inaccurate results
ATS: recent studies show that in those with darker skin pigments, pulse oximetry may miss below-normal oxygen saturations
OpenStax does not cover skin pigmentation in the pulse oximetry section read
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson includes one factual, attributed line noting skin pigmentation is a known accuracy factor and that a reading should be questioned when it does not fit the patient — without overclaiming or giving device guidance.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The phase-4 generated draft was generic boilerplate — 'Oxygen Saturation is a foundational concept in Nursing & Allied Health Foundations' — with no definition, range, measurement method, or clinical claims. Nothing in it survived the rewrite.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the boilerplate draft with a source-verified lesson: working definition attributed to MedlinePlus/NLM and corroborated by ATS and OpenStax; adult reference range 95-100% on room air attributed to MedlinePlus; measurement method verified against MedlinePlus, OpenStax, Merck Manual, and ATS; limits (cold fingers, dark nail polish, motion) verified against MedlinePlus and ATS; and the 'saturation, not total oxygen' framing verified against Merck Manual and the MedlinePlus ABG page.

sourceRecords.title: Pulse Oximetry (Medical Test)
sourceRecords.provider: MedlinePlus, U.S. National Library of Medicine (NIH)
sourceRecords.notes: Read directly 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200). Primary Tier A source. Supports: pulse oximetry as a test using a small clip-like device to measure blood oxygen; the normal oxygen saturation range of 95-100%; lower levels acceptable with COPD or pneumonia; lower readings at higher elevation; dark nail polish, artificial nails, darker skin pigmentation, poor circulation, and cold skin causing inaccurate results; results 2-4% higher or lower than the true value; hypoxemia risk and the 92%/88% consumer thresholds; cyanosis and other low-oxygen signs. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Clinical Nursing Skills (OpenStax)
sourceRecords.notes: Reused existing registry id and URL. Read 2026-08-22 from the official OpenStax PDF (Clinical-Nursing-Skills-WEB.pdf, published 2024-06-26). Supports: SpO2 as the saturation of hemoglobin with oxygen in peripheral blood; the pulse oximeter as a noninvasive finger device that reads hemoglobin saturation using light; normal saturation at sea level 94-98%; lower readings acceptable at elevation; COPD targets of 88-90% (ch. 18) and 88-92% (ch. 24); anemia as a lack of oxygen carriers; nail polish hindering readings; severe anemia, reduced extremity perfusion, and carbon monoxide exposure affecting accuracy; SpO2 as convenient but not always entirely accurate. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Arterial Blood Gas (ABG) Analysis and Pulse Oximetry (Consumer Version)
sourceRecords.notes: Read directly 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200; page dated Nov 2025). Tier B corroboration. Supports: pulse oximetry as noninvasive monitoring of blood oxygen with a sensor on a finger or earlobe, including continuous measurement; the arterial blood gas as a more exact measurement taken from an arterial blood sample that adds carbon dioxide and acidity; and the contrast between the two tests. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Pulse Oximetry (Patient Education Information Series)
sourceRecords.notes: Read directly 2026-08-22 (PDF, online version updated March 2021; Am J Respir Crit Care Med Vol. 184, P1-P2, 2011). Supports: oxygen saturation as the percentage of how much oxygen the blood is carrying compared to the maximum it is capable of carrying; beams of light passing through the finger to measure oxygen; low oxygen making cells unable to work properly; most oximeters reading about 2% over or under the true value; accuracy factors — cold hands, not holding still, nail polish (especially black, blue, green), artificial nails, thicker skin, skin pigment; smoking raising readings via carbon monoxide; the ABG contrast; best-reading guidance (warm, relaxed hand). Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.
